name: Mission San Diego de Alcalá
status: Active Catholic parish and minor basilica of the Diocese of San Diego
text: This is Mission San Diego de Alcalá, the first of California's 21 missions, founded on July 16, 1769. It began on a hill by the harbor and moved here in 1774, closer to Kumeyaay villages and water. The Kumeyaay have lived in this valley for thousands of years, and they live in San Diego County today.
more: Father Junípero Serra founded the mission in 1769 beside a new Spanish fort. Few Kumeyaay people joined at first. The California Indian Museum and Cultural Center counts only 26 baptisms in the first three years. On November 4 and 5, 1775, people from several Kumeyaay villages surrounded the mission and burned it. Father Luis Jayme was killed. He is buried by the altar and is remembered as California's first Christian martyr. Native accounts say violence by soldiers helped set off the revolt. At least 13 Kumeyaay people were jailed or killed afterward. The Spanish rebuilt the mission like a fort. Mexico ended the mission system in the 1830s. Today the Kumeyaay Nation includes twelve federally recognized bands in the United States.
visit: Plan about an hour. The church you see is the fifth on this site. It is a 1931 rebuild that copies the church dedicated in 1813, so the walls are not original. A single room, the Casa del Padre Serra, dates to 1774 and is believed to be the only original room that survived. Inside the church, look for Father Jayme's tomb near the altar. Outside stands a tall bell wall with five bells. The visitor center has a small museum, and the gardens are quiet. The mission's own website has a page on the Kumeyaay, and it is worth reading before you go. Easy to miss: the Casa del Padre Serra, tucked in with the museum rooms. This is a working parish, so be quiet during services. Hours and fees change and the grounds sometimes close for special events, so check before you go. The official page is linked in the app.

name: Carmel Mission
name_es: Misión San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo
status: Active Catholic parish and minor basilica of the Diocese of Monterey
wiki: Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo
text: This is Carmel Mission. Father Junípero Serra founded it at Monterey in 1770 and moved it here in 1771. It was his headquarters until he died in 1784, and he is buried in the church. This is the homeland of the Rumsen Ohlone and the Esselen, whose descendants still live in this region.
more: Serra moved the mission here from Monterey, partly to keep Native people away from the soldiers. He led all the missions from this place until he died on August 28, 1784. He is buried beneath the sanctuary floor. Esselen and Rumsen Ohlone people were baptized here, moved to the mission and put to work. About 900 Esselen people were baptized and brought to missions in this region. Disease, hunger and overwork killed many. Pope Francis canonized Serra on September 23, 2015. Many Catholics honor him as a saint. Many Native Californians objected, saying he stands for the system that broke their families, and this mission was vandalized days later. In 2020 the Esselen Tribe of Monterey County regained 1,199 acres of its homeland near Big Sur.
visit: Plan one to two hours. The stone church was finished in 1797 and its walls are original. Its roof fell in 1852, and the church stood open to the sky for about thirty years until repairs began in 1884. A restorer named Harry Downie then worked here for about fifty years, so much of what you see has been carefully rebuilt. Pope John the Twenty-third made it a minor basilica in 1960. Four small museums cover mission life, the Munras family and Serra's own simple cell in the convento. A chapel gallery holds a 1924 monument to Serra. The cemetery and gardens are peaceful. Easy to miss: Serra's cell in the convento museum. This is an active parish, so some areas close during Mass. Hours and fees change, and the mission has been closed on some weekdays, so check before you go. The official page is linked in the app.

name: Mission San Antonio de Padua
status: Catholic parish church, museum and retreat center of the Diocese of Monterey, inside Fort Hunter Liggett
text: This is Mission San Antonio de Padua, the third mission, founded by Serra on July 14, 1771. It moved to this spot in 1773 for a steadier water supply. It sits in the homeland of the Salinan people, and the Salinan Tribe helps care for the cemetery here today.
more: San Antonio was among the first places in Alta California to make fired red clay roof tiles, which protected buildings from fire. Its builders also dug a system of channels from the San Antonio River, and its remains are described as the most complete mission water system in California. Salinan people did the farming and building, and once baptized they were not free to leave. After Mexico ended the mission system in the 1830s, the church fell into ruin. It was rebuilt in the twentieth century. In World War Two the Army took over the surrounding ranch land, so the mission now sits inside a military base. The Salinan Tribe of Monterey and San Luis Obispo Counties restored the cemetery wall, which honors about 3,000 ancestors. The tribe is seeking federal recognition.
visit: This is the most remote mission on the list, so plan half a day. You reach it from Highway 101 by about 26 miles of Jolon Road, then about six more miles of Mission Road inside Fort Hunter Liggett. The base has its own gate rules, so read the mission's directions page first. The church was begun in 1810, fell into ruin and was rebuilt in the twentieth century. It is a reconstruction on the original plan. The museum holds Native American and mission-era archaeology and is the best stop for the Salinan story. Walk out to the remains of the water system, which are original and easy to overlook. There is also a gift shop and a retreat center, and fiestas are held on the grounds. Easy to miss: the water system ruins beyond the church. Hours and fees change, and the mission has posted holiday closures, so check before you go. The official page is linked in the app.

name: Mission San Gabriel
founder: Fathers Pedro Benito Cambón and Ángel Fernández de la Somera, under Junípero Serra's authority
people: Tongva (some descendants use the name Kizh)
status: Active Catholic parish of the Archdiocese of Los Angeles, run by the Claretian Missionaries, with a museum
text: This is Mission San Gabriel, founded on September 8, 1771 and moved here a few years later after floods. It stands in the homeland of the Tongva people, and some of their descendants use the name Kizh. Nearly 6,000 Native people are buried on these grounds.
more: Fathers Pedro Benito Cambón and Ángel Fernández de la Somera founded the mission, under Serra's authority. In 1782 the governor ordered soldiers to stop baptized Tongva people from holding their dances. In 1785 a medicine woman named Toypurina helped organize a revolt. It failed. She was convicted, baptized under pressure and sent far away, and she died in 1799. Her descendants are enrolled in the Kizh Nation today. The mission museum names 7,054 Native people baptized here from 1771 to 1848. A missionary of the time reported that three of every four children died before the age of two. An arson fire destroyed the church roof on July 11, 2020. The museum reopened in 2023 with an exhibit on Native history.
visit: Plan one to two hours. The church was finished in 1805 and its walls are original. The roof burned in 2020 and was rebuilt, so look up to see the new work. The church is unlike the other missions. Its architect, Father Antonio Cruzado, gave it tall narrow windows and capped buttresses, a style the California Missions Foundation ties to the cathedral of Córdoba in Spain. The earthquake of December 8, 1812 toppled the first bell tower, and the six-bell wall beside the church replaced it. The museum has the 2023 exhibit on Native people, the missionaries and the birth of Los Angeles. Easy to miss: the Wall of Names, which lists Native people baptized here. The cemetery and gardens are quiet, and the Claretian Missionaries still run this as a parish. The official site sometimes blocks automated readers, so confirm hours and fees by phone or on the site before you go. The official page is linked in the app.

name: Mission San Luis Obispo
name_es: Misión San Luis Obispo de Tolosa
status: Active Catholic parish (Old Mission Parish) of the Diocese of Monterey, with a museum
wiki: Mission San Luis Obispo de Tolosa
text: This is Mission San Luis Obispo, the fifth mission, founded by Serra on September 1, 1772, beside San Luis Creek. It stands in Northern Chumash homeland, and Chumash people still live in this region. Its church is the only L-shaped church among the California missions.
more: In 1772 the soldiers and priests at Monterey were short of food. Serra sent a hunting party to this valley, and the hunters brought back so much bear meat that he chose it for a mission. Father José Cavaller built it with Chumash labor. Once people were baptized they were not free to leave. In 1776 a flaming arrow set the mission's thatched roofs on fire. The padres then began firing clay roof tiles here,. The last Franciscan of the era died in 1842, and the buildings decayed. In 2020 the Diocese of Monterey took down a statue of Serra at the mission. One Northern Chumash tribe calls San Luis Obispo its cultural capital. The Salinan Tribe also claims part of this region, and the two disagree.
visit: Plan about an hour. The church and convento are original, from the 1790s. In the 1880s the buildings were remodeled in a New England style. That remodel was undone in the 1930s, so what you see is a restoration. The church is L-shaped, with a long second nave beside the main one. The old convento once held the first county courthouse and jail. The church doors are open every day, and a small museum and gift shop sit beside it. Docent tours run on a posted schedule. Out front, Mission Plaza slopes down to the creek and has a bronze grizzly bear. Easy to miss: the second nave, which makes the L. The mission is still a working parish. Hours and fees change, so check before you go. The official page is linked in the app.

name: Mission Dolores
founder: Father Francisco Palóu, with Father Pedro Benito Cambón, under Junípero Serra's authority
people: Ramaytush Ohlone (the Yelamu group), with Coast Miwok and others brought later
status: Active Catholic parish of the Archdiocese of San Francisco; the old chapel is a museum
text: This is Mission Dolores in San Francisco. The first Mass here was said on June 29, 1776. The little adobe chapel beside the big church, finished in 1791, is the oldest intact building in the city. This is the homeland of the Ramaytush Ohlone, who are still here.
more: Father Francisco Palóu founded the mission with Father Pedro Benito Cambón. Serra was not there. The mission counts June 29, 1776 as the first Mass and October 9 as the formal dedication. The Ohlone provided most of the labor that built the adobe chapel. People from the Yelamu, the Ramaytush Ohlone group of this peninsula, joined the mission. Coast Miwok and others were brought from farther away. Conditions were hard and disease spread. By 1832 more than 5,000 Native people had died here, says the California Missions Foundation. At its peak about 1,100 Native people lived at the mission. The cemetery holds Ohlone, Miwok and other First Californians. Today an Ohlone garden grows on the grounds, and the Association of Ramaytush Ohlone speaks for the original peoples of the Peninsula.
visit: Plan 45 minutes to an hour. The adobe chapel is original, finished in 1791, and it survived the 1906 earthquake. The ceiling still shows Ohlone designs painted in plant dyes. The brick church built next door in 1876 did not survive 1906. The tall basilica you see beside the chapel was finished in 1918 and became a minor basilica in 1952. A small museum explains mission life, and the walk-through is self guided. The cemetery holds early California leaders and about 5,000 Native people. Easy to miss: the Ohlone garden of native plants in the grounds. The mission is a living parish with Mass on a schedule. Hours change, and guided tours have been paused, so check before you go. The official page is linked in the app.

name: Mission San Juan Capistrano
founder: Junípero Serra, on All Saints' Day 1776, after a first attempt by Fermín Lasuén in 1775
status: Mission museum and historic landmark; the Serra Chapel is part of the mission parish (Diocese of Orange); a separate modern basilica stands next door
text: This is Mission San Juan Capistrano, founded on November 1, 1776, after a first try in 1775 was abandoned within days. This is Acjachemen homeland. The Serra Chapel, finished in 1782, is regarded as the oldest building in California still in use. The mission is famous for its swallows.
more: Father Fermín Lasuén raised a cross here on October 30, 1775. When word came that Kumeyaay people had burned Mission San Diego, the priests buried the bells and left. Serra returned and founded the mission on All Saints' Day, 1776. The Acjachemen lived in villages along these creeks, and the large village of Putuidem lay about a mile north. About 4,600 Native people were baptized here between 1776 and 1847. Construction of the Great Stone Church needed the labor of the whole Native community. It collapsed in the earthquake of December 8, 1812, during Mass, and about 40 people died. The ruins still stand. Mexico ended the mission system in 1833. Acjachemen families still live in this region and keep their language and traditions alive.
visit: Plan one and a half to two hours. The Serra Chapel is original, from 1782, restored in the early 1900s. It holds a gilded Baroque altarpiece and is the last church where Serra is known to have said Mass. The Great Stone Church was begun in 1797 and finished in 1806, and what you see now are its ruins, kept as ruins. The grounds also have gardens, a bell wall, a museum and the old cemetery. The big modern church next door is a separate basilica. The swallows are celebrated each year on March 19, but they spend only part of the year here. Easy to miss: the quiet old cemetery, where mission-era people were buried. The Serra Chapel still serves the parish, so some visits are limited during services. Hours and fees change, and the mission closes for some events, so check before you go. The official page is linked in the app.

name: Mission Santa Clara
founder: Father Tomás de la Peña, under Junípero Serra's authority
status: Chapel and parish church of Santa Clara University (Jesuit); open to visitors
text: This is Mission Santa Clara, founded on January 12, 1777, the first California mission named for a woman. It stands on the campus of Santa Clara University, in the homeland of the Tamien Ohlone. The church you see is a re-creation built after a fire in 1926.
more: Father Tomás de la Peña said the first Mass at the Tamien village of So-co-is-u-ka on the Guadalupe River. Floods, fires and earthquakes forced the mission to move, and it now stands on its fifth site. Tamien Ohlone people were baptized and put to work here, and Bay Miwok and Yokuts people joined them later. King Charles the Third of Spain sent bells in 1777 and asked that they be rung each evening in memory of the dead. After Mexico ended the system in 1833, most of the land and livestock were sold. In 1851 the Jesuits took over and opened a college, now Santa Clara University, the oldest university in California. In 2023 the university announced a partnership with the Muwekma Ohlone Tribe. The Tamien Nation also traces its roots to this valley.
visit: Plan 45 minutes. This is the only mission on a university campus. The church was rebuilt in 1928 and 1929 to re-create the 1825 church that burned in October 1926, so it is a replica. The mission gardens on campus are open for a quiet walk. The university offers a self-guided walking tour of the mission grounds and a virtual tour. The bell tower holds bells cast in different years, including one given by King Alfonso the Thirteenth of Spain in 1929. Easy to miss: the mission gardens, tucked among the campus paths. The church is open every day. It is also a working chapel, so some hours are set aside for services. Check before you go. The official page is linked in the app.

name: Mission San Buenaventura
founder: Junípero Serra, the last mission he founded
status: Active Catholic parish and minor basilica of the Archdiocese of Los Angeles, with a museum
text: This is Mission San Buenaventura in Ventura, founded by Serra on Easter Sunday, March 31, 1782. It was the last mission he founded. This is Chumash homeland, and Chumash people still live along this coast.
more: Serra planned this mission early, but it became the ninth. Chumash people, who lived in villages along the coast and the river, were baptized and kept at the mission to work its fields and herds. Between 1805 and 1815 they built a seven-mile aqueduct of earth and stone from the Ventura River. The church was dedicated in 1809. The earthquakes of 1812 and a wave from the sea sent the friars and Chumash people inland for a time. Mexico ended the mission system in 1834. In 2020 the city of Ventura took down its Serra statue, and in 2024 the statue was given a home at the mission. Pope Francis named the church a minor basilica in 2020. Descendants include the Barbareño Ventureño Band of Chumash Indians.
visit: Plan about an hour. The church was dedicated in 1809, and its walls are original. In 1893 a remodel painted over its old decoration, and a careful restoration was finished in 1957. A small museum holds two wooden bells, the only wooden bells known from any California mission. They were rung during Holy Week, when the metal bells were silent. The museum also shows Chumash and mission-era objects. A thirty-minute video tells the history, and the garden has a grotto. The mission sits on Main Street in downtown Ventura, so it is easy to pair with a walk. Easy to miss: the wooden bells in the museum. The mission is a living parish, so be quiet during Mass. Tour times and prices change, so check before you go. The official page is linked in the app.

name: Old Mission Santa Barbara
status: Active parish of the Archdiocese of Los Angeles, where Franciscan friars have lived since 1786; museum
text: This is Old Mission Santa Barbara, called the Queen of the Missions, founded on December 4, 1786. Franciscan friars have lived here without a break since the day it was founded. This is Chumash homeland, and Barbareño Chumash people are still here.
more: Father Fermín Lasuén founded the mission on the feast of Saint Barbara. The mission's herds disrupted the Chumash way of hunting and gathering, and epidemics struck people who had no immunity. In 1803 a record 1,792 Chumash people lived in adobe huts around the mission. By 1820 the number had fallen to 1,132, and by 1823 to 962. In February 1824 a soldier beat a Chumash man at Mission Santa Inés, and a revolt spread across the region. At Santa Barbara, Chumash people led by Andrés Sagimomatsee seized the mission. Many later withdrew into the interior mountains. About 4,000 Chumash people are buried in the mission cemetery. Today the mission offers space for classes in the Barbareño Chumash language.
visit: Plan about an hour and a half. The earthquake of December 21, 1812 destroyed the third church. The stone church you see was built from about 1815 to 1820, so the walls are original. A 1925 earthquake damaged the twin towers, and the facade and towers were taken down and rebuilt in their original form from 1950 to 1953. The museum fills nine rooms, and the gardens cover fifteen acres. Near the entrance stand the original fountain and the lavadero, a stone basin where women washed clothes. An audio tour comes in six languages. The cemetery holds both Chumash and Spanish-era graves. Easy to miss: Mission Historical Park across the street, with remains of the aqueduct and reservoir. The church is a living parish, so parts close for services, weddings and funerals. Hours and fees change, so check before you go. The official page is linked in the app.

name: La Purísima Mission
status: La Purísima Mission State Historic Park, run by California State Parks; not a parish church
text: This is La Purísima Mission, founded on December 8, 1787. An earthquake and floods destroyed the first mission in 1812, and it was re-founded on this site in 1813. Today it is a state historic park, and Chumash people still live in this region.
more: Father Fermín Lasuén founded the mission at a Chumash place called Algsacpi, near today's downtown Lompoc. By 1803 about 1,436 Chumash people lived under mission control. The earthquake and heavy rains of December 21, 1812 destroyed the buildings. The mission was re-founded on April 23, 1813 at this new site. In February 1824 a revolt that began at Mission Santa Inés spread here, and Chumash people took over La Purísima and held it for about a month. After Mexico ended the mission system, the buildings were abandoned and fell into ruin. The Civilian Conservation Corps began rebuilding the mission from the ruins in 1934. It was dedicated on December 7, 1941, the day Pearl Harbor was attacked. The nearest federally recognized Chumash tribe is the Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians.
visit: Plan a half day. State Parks calls this the most completely restored mission in California. It is a reconstruction, built from ruins by Civilian Conservation Corps crews from 1934 to 1941, so the walls are not original. The church and the padre's chapel stand with ten restored and furnished buildings, including shops, living quarters and a blacksmith. There is a five-acre garden, and the corrals hold burros, horses, longhorn cattle, sheep and goats. The visitor center has exhibits, and trails and horseback rides cross the hills. Easy to miss: the ruins of the first mission site in Lompoc, at 508 South F Street. This is not a church, so you can wander at your own pace. It is a state park, so check hours and fees before you go. The official page is linked in the app.

name: Mission Santa Cruz
people: Awaswas-speaking Ohlone (the Uypi people) and Yokuts
status: Replica chapel of Holy Cross Parish (Diocese of Monterey); the surviving adobe is Santa Cruz Mission State Historic Park
text: This is Mission Santa Cruz, founded on August 28, 1791, the only mission named for the Holy Cross. This is the homeland of the Awaswas-speaking Ohlone, the Uypi people. Only one original building survives, an adobe that housed Native families.
more: Father Fermín Lasuén raised the cross on August 28, 1791. Floods soon moved the mission up to Mission Hill. In 1797 Spanish officials founded a town across the river, to the priests' displeasure. On October 12, 1812, Father Andrés Quintana was killed by Native workers. A man named Lorenzo Asisara, whose father took part, later told the story. The workers acted after Quintana punished them with a metal-tipped whip, and they strangled him. The one surviving mission building is an adobe built from 1822 to 1824 for Native families, Yokuts and Ohlone, who lived here. State Parks says it is the only building of its kind still standing in California. The Uypi people are ancestral relatives of the Amah Mutsun Tribal Band.
visit: Plan about an hour, in two stops. The chapel on High Street is a replica finished in 1931. It follows an 1876 painting and is about one third the size of the original church. The Holy Cross Church from 1889 stands over part of the old church. A short walk away on School Street is the real survivor, the adobe built from 1822 to 1824 to house Native families. It is part of Santa Cruz Mission State Historic Park, and its exhibits tell the Ohlone and Yokuts story. The old church lost its front wall in the earthquake of 1857. Easy to miss: the adobe on School Street, a short walk from the chapel. The mission was nicknamed the hard-luck mission for its floods and quakes. The chapel is a parish building, so hours differ from the park. Check before you go. The official page is linked in the app.

name: Mission Soledad
name_es: Misión Nuestra Señora de la Soledad
people: Chalon Ohlone, with Esselen, Salinan and Yokuts people brought later
status: Chapel and museum of Our Lady of Solitude parish (Diocese of Monterey); not state funded and relies on donations
wiki: Mission Nuestra Señora de la Soledad
text: This is Mission Soledad, founded on October 9, 1791 in the Salinas Valley. Its name means solitude. The Chalon Ohlone lived here first, and Esselen and Yokuts people were brought here later. The chapel you see was rebuilt in 1955.
more: Father Fermín Lasuén founded the mission. The Chalon, a group of Ohlone, were baptized and lived here first, followed by Esselen and Yokuts people. By 1803 there were 627 Native people at the mission. About 900 Esselen people in all were baptized and brought to the missions around their homeland, including Carmel, Soledad and San Antonio. The Salinas River flooded the mission in 1824, 1828 and 1832. Governor José Joaquín de Arrillaga died here on July 24, 1814 and was buried in the chapel. After Mexico ended the mission system, the mission was sold for a reported 800 dollars, stripped for building materials and left in ruins. The Native Daughters of the Golden West rebuilt the chapel, dedicated on October 9, 1955. Esselen and Ohlone descendants still live in this region.
visit: Plan 45 minutes. The mission sits about three miles off Highway 101. The small chapel you enter is a rebuild from the 1950s, so it is not original. The long adobe ruins beside it are original. They are the unrestored walls of the old quadrangle. A museum in the convento wing displays mission-era objects, including an old mission bell. The cemetery holds a marker for Governor Arrillaga. There is a gift shop, and the tour is self guided. Easy to miss: the adobe ruins behind the chapel, which show the old layout. The mission is not funded by the state and depends on donations. Hours change, and the mission closes on Mondays and some holidays, so check before you go. The official page is linked in the app.

name: Mission San José
people: Ohlone (Chochenyo speakers), with Bay Miwok, Yokuts, Plains Miwok and others brought later
status: Catholic church of Saint Joseph Parish (Diocese of Oakland), with a museum
text: This is Mission San José in Fremont, founded on June 11, 1797 at the Ohlone village of Oroysom. It is not in the city of San Jose. The church you see is a 1985 replica. This is Ohlone homeland, and Ohlone people live in the Bay Area today.
more: Father Fermín Lasuén founded the mission. Native people from Mission Santa Clara did the first building. Many Ohlone had been baptized at Santa Clara and came home to form the founding community. A measles epidemic in 1806 killed about a quarter of the mission's people. Newcomers from farther away then joined, and by the 1830s Plains Miwok was the main Native language here. Father Narciso Durán trained a Native choir and a thirty-piece orchestra that became famous across California. Estanislao, a Yokuts man from the Stanislaus River, was a Native community leader here. He left with about 400 followers in 1827 and led an uprising in 1828. After secularization many Native people fled but could not return to their old way of life, and many died of disease and hunger.
visit: Plan about an hour. The church is a replica of the 1809 adobe church. The Hayward Fault earthquake of October 21, 1868 shattered the original, and the replica was built from 1982 to 1985. The museum is in a surviving original adobe wing, one of the few old buildings left. You enter the cemetery through the museum. The grounds are free to walk. Inside the church, the original hammered copper baptismal font has been returned, along with the bell wheel the Ohlone used during the sacred parts of Mass. Easy to miss: that baptismal font and the bell wheel. The mission is the church of a busy parish, so it may close for services. Tours by reservation have been offered on one weekend each month. Hours change, and the mission has closed on Mondays and Tuesdays, so check before you go. The official page is linked in the app.

name: Mission San Juan Bautista
people: Mutsun Ohlone, with Yokuts people brought later
status: Active Catholic parish of the Diocese of Monterey, facing the plaza of San Juan Bautista State Historic Park
text: This is Mission San Juan Bautista, founded on June 24, 1797, and nicknamed the Mission of Music. It stands beside the San Andreas Fault, in the homeland of the Mutsun Ohlone. Its church is the only one among the California missions with three aisles.
more: Father Fermín Lasuén founded the mission on the feast of Saint John the Baptist. The Mutsun Ohlone, the original residents of the valley, were baptized and brought to live here, followed by Yokuts people from the Central Valley. Father Estevan Tapis taught a Native boys' choir with color-coded music notation, which earned the mission its nickname. The mission was secularized in 1835 and reconsecrated as a parish in 1859. On December 22, 2012, the Bishop of Monterey led a Mass of Reconciliation here, asking forgiveness of the Amah Mutsun, the descendants of the Mutsun. The Amah Mutsun Tribal Band is seeking federal recognition. A second group also uses the Amah Mutsun name, so ask each group how it names itself.
visit: Plan about an hour and a half. The church dates from the early 1800s and has three aisles. The side aisles were walled in after earthquake damage in 1812 and reopened in 1975, so the church is close to its old design. The San Andreas Fault runs just below the cemetery wall, and the earthquake of 1906 ruined the outer walls. Below the wall you can walk a preserved stretch of the old El Camino Real. The mission's museum, garden and cemetery are open, and the plaza buildings of the state historic park face the church. The mission appeared in Alfred Hitchcock's 1958 film Vertigo, and the studio added the bell tower you see in the movie. Easy to miss: the El Camino Real path below the cemetery. Hours and fees differ from the state park's, so check before you go. The official page is linked in the app.

name: Mission San Miguel
status: Active Catholic parish of the Diocese of Monterey, with a museum
text: This is Mission San Miguel, founded on July 25, 1797, in Salinan homeland. Its church, finished in 1818, still has its original painted walls, which have never been repainted. Salinan people are still here, and this place is part of their story.
more: Father Fermín Lasuén founded the mission to close the gap between San Antonio and San Luis Obispo. The site was chosen because many Salinan people lived nearby, close to a village called Vahca. A fire destroyed the first church in 1806. The church you see was built from 1816 to 1818, and its bright interior was painted by Native people under the supervision of Esteban Munras, a Spanish artist. It has never been repainted. About 2,000 Native people are buried in the cemetery outside. After Mexico ended the mission system, the mission buildings were sold off, and several became shops, hotels and saloons. The Franciscans returned in 1928. The San Simeon earthquake of December 22, 2003 closed the church for six years, and it reopened in 2009.
visit: Plan about an hour. This is the place to see what a mission church really looked like inside. The church, built from 1816 to 1818, is original, and the painted walls have never been redone. The walls are six feet thick. The 2003 earthquake severely damaged the church, and it was repaired. Beside the church stand the original arcade and the old padres' quarters. A museum and gift shop sit nearby, and the cemetery lies outside. Just south of the mission is the Rios-Caledonia Adobe, a house museum from 1835. Easy to miss: the bright painted patterns on the walls, which are the work of Native artists. This is a working parish, so be quiet during Mass. The mission's own website blocks some readers, so use the link in the app and confirm hours and fees by phone before you go.

name: Mission San Fernando
name_es: Misión San Fernando Rey de España
status: Archdiocese of Los Angeles; the convento grounds are a museum and the church is a chapel
wiki: Mission San Fernando Rey de España
text: This is Mission San Fernando, founded on September 8, 1797, at the settlement of Achooykomenga. The long convento, finished in 1822, still stands. The mission gave its name to the San Fernando Valley. The Fernandeño Tataviam Band descends from people who lived at this mission.
more: Father Fermín Lasuén founded the mission on a farming settlement called Achooykomenga, worked by Ventureño Chumash, Tongva and Tataviam laborers. The Tongva people brought here are known as Fernandeño. In the first decade of the 1800s the mission's Native population grew from 310 to 955, but the records show 1,468 baptisms and 797 deaths in those same ten years. The convento took twelve years to build and was finished in 1822. Mexico secularized the mission in 1834, and it returned to the Catholic Church in 1861. The 1971 earthquake destroyed the church, and it was rebuilt by 1974. The Fernandeño Tataviam Band of Mission Indians is working toward federal recognition.
visit: Plan about an hour. The convento is the long building you see first. It was a guesthouse for travelers on El Camino Real, finished in 1822, and it is original. It has a colonnade of nineteen arches. The church beside it is not original. The 1971 San Fernando earthquake destroyed it and it was rebuilt by 1974 and its walls carry designs inspired by Native patterns. In the courtyard stands a fountain described as original, modeled on one in Córdoba, Spain. The winery is a replica. Bob Hope and his wife Dolores are buried in the memorial garden. Easy to miss: the convento rooms, which hold relics and furniture from the old days. The mission asks you to call to confirm hours, and it closes on some holidays, so check before you go. The official page is linked in the app.

name: Mission San Luis Rey
name_es: Misión San Luis Rey de Francia
status: Parish, museum and retreat center run by the Franciscan Friars (Diocese of San Diego)
wiki: Mission San Luis Rey de Francia
text: This is Mission San Luis Rey, nicknamed the King of the Missions, founded on June 13, 1798. It gave its name to the Luiseño people, who call themselves the Payómkawichum. At its peak, it was the largest mission in California.
more: Father Fermín Lasuén founded the mission, and it became the biggest in the chain. In 1825 it held 2,869 people, and it ran about 26,000 cattle. Pablo Tac was born here around 1822. A priest took him to Rome as a boy, and there he wrote down the Luiseño language and the story of his people. He wrote that in his home village of Quechla there had been 5,000 people, until a sickness killed 2,000 of them. He died in Rome in 1841. The church finished in 1815 is the only surviving mission church built in the shape of a cross. After Mexico ended the mission system, services stopped until 1893. Today six federally recognized Luiseño tribes have reservations in Southern California, and Luiseño language revival is under way.
visit: Plan an hour and a half. The church was finished in 1815, with a wooden dome and cupola, and it has been restored since 1893. It is the only surviving mission church built in the shape of a cross. Outside, the quadrangle holds the soldiers' barracks, the lavandería where clothes were washed, a kiln and the first pepper tree planted in California, in 1830. The museum and the Madonna Chapel are on site, and the original cemetery dates from 1798. A free phone tour is called the King of the Missions app. Easy to miss: the lavandería and the kiln, at the edge of the grounds. Farther inland stands the Pala asistencia, from 1816, on the Pala Reservation. This is a living parish and retreat center, so some areas close for services. Hours and fees change, so check before you go. The official page is linked in the app.

name: Mission Santa Inés
status: Active Catholic parish of the Archdiocese of Los Angeles, served by Capuchin Franciscan friars since 1924; museum
text: This is Mission Santa Inés in Solvang, founded on September 17, 1804. The Chumash revolt of 1824 began here. This is Chumash homeland, and the Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians lives in this valley today.
more: Father Estevan Tapis founded the mission. The earthquake of December 21, 1812 destroyed most of the first church, and the present church was dedicated on July 4, 1817. On February 21, 1824, a soldier beat a young Chumash man here, and people rose up. The revolt spread to La Purísima and Santa Barbara, and Chumash people burned parts of this mission. Many then left for the interior mountains, and only a few stayed. The mission was secularized in 1835. In 1844 California's first college seminary opened here. Later the Danish town of Solvang grew up around the mission. Today the Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians, a federally recognized tribe, has its home in the valley and runs a museum and cultural center in Santa Ynez.
visit: Plan about an hour. The church was dedicated in 1817 and its walls are original. Repairs began in 1904 and a major restoration followed from 1947, so you are seeing a church that has been carefully maintained rather than left alone. The museum holds vestments, art, old manuscripts and bells. The mission garden and the rose garden are good places to sit. A gift shop is on site, and docent tours can be reserved. Capuchin Franciscan friars have served the parish since 1924. The mission sits at the edge of Solvang, so the Danish shops of the town are close by. Easy to miss: the old bells and manuscripts in the museum. For the Chumash story, add the Santa Ynez Band's museum and cultural center in nearby Santa Ynez. Hours and fees change, so check before you go. The official page is linked in the app.

name: Mission San Rafael
status: Replica chapel of Saint Raphael Parish (Archdiocese of San Francisco)
text: This is Mission San Rafael, founded on December 14, 1817 as a hospital outpost of Mission Dolores for sick Native people. This is Coast Miwok homeland, and the Coast Miwok are still here. The chapel you see is a replica from 1949.
more: Father Vicente Francisco de Sarría founded San Rafael as an asistencia of Mission Dolores. It was meant to heal Native people who were sick in foggy San Francisco, and it is called Alta California's first sanitarium. It was named for the archangel of healing. It became a full mission on October 19, 1822. In 1835 its population was reported at 1,027. After Mexico ended the mission system, the mission was abandoned, and the last ruins were removed by 1870. John Frémont used the site as a headquarters during the Bear Flag Revolt of 1846. On October 12, 2020, a protest organized by Coast Miwok people toppled a Serra statue here. The Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria, Coast Miwok and Southern Pomo, was restored by Congress in 2000.
visit: Plan 30 to 45 minutes. Nothing original survives here, since the ruins were cleared away by 1870. The chapel you visit was built in 1949 near the site of the original hospital, with help from a foundation. It stands next to the parish church. A small museum and gift shop sit on the grounds, but their hours are not posted online, so call the parish office. The chapel's star-shaped window is a Moorish-style detail like one at Carmel. The replica chapel is one of the smallest churches in the chain. The chapel is part of a working parish, so it may be closed during services. Easy to miss: the bell and sign put up in 1909 by the Native Sons of the Golden West to mark the original site. For Coast Miwok history, ask at the parish office or visit the Graton Rancheria's website. Check hours before you go. The official page is linked in the app.

name: Sonoma Mission
people: Coast Miwok, Southern Pomo, Wappo and Patwin
status: Museum in Sonoma State Historic Park, run by California State Parks; not a church
text: This is Sonoma Mission, the last and northernmost of the 21 missions, founded on July 4, 1823. It is the only one founded after Mexico won independence from Spain. This is the homeland of the Coast Miwok, Southern Pomo, Wappo and Patwin peoples.
more: Father José Altimira founded the mission, with soldiers and Native people moved from Mission Dolores. Its first report listed no baptisms and 482 Native people, all transferred from other missions. Governor Luis Argüello backed the mission partly to block Russian expansion from Fort Ross. In 1826 Native people who lived outside the mission were unhappy about their share of the harvest and burned some of the wooden buildings. Altimira fled. Mariano Vallejo later administered the mission, and the adobe chapel was built in 1841 on his orders. A memorial dedicated in 1999 honors more than 800 Native people, including over 200 children, who died at the mission between 1824 and 1839. Their descendants include members of the Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria.
visit: Plan an hour, or half a day with the rest of the park. This is a museum, not a church. The adobe chapel dates from 1841. The buildings were reconstructed by 1913 and remodeled later, so they are old walls with newer work. Inside, the museum shows the paintings of Chris Jorgensen, who painted the California missions. Outside stands the Sonoma Mission Indian Memorial, which honors the Native people who died here. The same state park includes the Sonoma Barracks and Vallejo's home, all around the town plaza. The Bear Flag was first raised near here in 1846. Easy to miss: the memorial to the Native people, off to one side. Hours and fees are posted by State Parks, so check before you go. The official page is linked in the app.
